transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-10-21 16:00 UTC | Duration: 45 minutes | Recording: yes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Reyes (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (CoreFin CTO), Gavin Lee (CoreFin SRE), Anita Patel (CoreFin Product)

Summary: Quick sync to review last week's pilot numbers, validate burst runbook ideas, and align on autoscale cooldowns. Focus on dedicated reserve + transient burst policy and acceptable latency/cost tradeoffs.

[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:04] Priya: Priya here.
[00:05] Gavin: Gavin.
[00:06] Anita: Anita.
[00:07] Marco: Marco from Redwood.
[00:09] Lena: Great. We'll run through the pilot metrics Marco pulled, then talk burst options and fallbacks.

[02:10] Marco: Alright, so for the 48 hour sample we ran last week, average QPS was around 120, peak 700 for short bursts. P50 token latency on the dedicated worker is about 60ms, P95 sits at 420ms, P99 around 1.2s. Note those peaks lines up with KV cache misses and prefixes longer than our 512 token warm paths.

[04:05] Priya: Sorry can you repeat the P95? 420... is that milliseconds?
[04:08] Marco: Yeah, 420ms P95. The P99 was higher, that's when the model had to re-prime the KV cache. Also we saw that when sequence length increases the kernel selection moved to the slower path — that was the biggest contributor.

[06:25] Gavin: On our side we've seen some network blips around 02:00 UTC that coincide with higher egress on the subnet, suspecting an upstream batch job. If bursts coincide it's rough. We need a runway where a burst doesn't break the SLA.

[08:30] Lena: That's where the dedicated reserve + burst policy comes in — you keep a baseline reserved capacity for steady QPS and allow policy-triggered burst capacity. We support a priority queue so pilot traffic can preempt lower priority tenants in the same pool, plus automated fallback to a small quantized variant if latency spikes.

[09:15] Anita: The quantized variant, are we seeing accuracy regressions with that? CoreFin can't degrade transaction classification quality beyond 1.5% precision loss.
[09:22] Marco: Good call. In our tests the 4-bit quantized variant added about 0.8-1.2% delta on the classification evals with your probe prompt set. But for some long-context flows the syntactic outputs change — it's not just precision. We'll run a targeted eval against your regression suite.

[11:50] Priya: We need concrete numbers for cost vs latency if we do reserve 4 GPUs vs reserve 2 + burst. Can you show scenario math?
[11:57] Lena: Yes — I'll send the cost scenarios. Quick run here: reserve 2 GPUs gives a steady baseline and autoscale can add up to 6 for burst. The unit-cost when bursting is higher per token but amortized. We'll show the math in the follow-up.

[14:05] Marco: About autoscale: default cooldown we used was 120s on scale-out and 300s on scale-in. That avoids flapping but increases tail in some fast-surge cases. We can add a predictive ramp using short-term moving-average so we can pre-warm capacity if we detect a ramp.

[15:12] Gavin: How does predictive ramping affect cost? If we pre-warm we bill for the reserve until the burst actually hits, right?
[15:18] Marco: We recommend a hybrid — small pre-warm (1-2 nodes) for anticipated surges and then rapid add for the remaining. We only charge for active nodes; we can configure autoscale so pre-warm is ephemeral and integrated with the burst reservation window.

[17:30] Priya: On security: we need VPC peering and KMS/HSM key rotation patterns. Also audit logs with token-level tracing for a 90 day retention. Are these available in the private plane?
[17:42] Lena: Yes — Dedicated supports VPC peering and the Private control plane has KMS integrations and audit trails. We can export audit logs to your SIEM. For token-level export, we have redaction controls; we don't export raw user-provided PII by default.

[19:05] Anita: What's the fallback sequence during a heavy burst? Can you outline the runbook?
[19:11] Marco: Sure. Typical sequence: 1) Priority routing - pilot traffic goes to reserved pool. 2) If reserved saturated, attempt burst allocation up to agreed burst cap. 3) If burst capacity isn't available or latency beyond threshold, route to quantized model variant in same pool. 4) If still failing, route to hosted lightweight model (higher cost but more elastic) as last resort. All transitions logged and we can attach reason codes for tracing.

[22:00] Priya: For step 3, we worry about functional regressions. Can we gate fallback with a live canary eval — only roll traffic to quantized variant if recent sample responses pass a smoke-check?
[22:10] Marco: Yes you can. We support a canary gating hook: run N sample prompts through the candidate variant and compare metrics (top-k overlap, confidence). If it passes thresholds you failover, otherwise continue to hosted fallback. There's a small time cost for the gate — usually 2-4s.

[25:00] Gavin: One operational ask: we want a 'burst dry-run' window where a simulated ramp exercises the policy without touching production traffic. Can you do that?
[25:07] Lena: Absolutely — Marco can run a synthetic replay of your trace against the pilot config and we'll produce a runbook readout showing how autoscale and fallbacks would have acted.

[27:30] Marco: I'll need a 90-day representative traffic trace (anonymized) and your prompt mix distribution. If you can't provide 90 days we can use 7-14 days plus synthetic amplifications. We'll produce: load vs node count, P95/P99 latencies, KV cache hit scenarios, and a cost delta matrix for reserve vs reserve+burst vs reserve+hosted fallback.

[29:40] Priya: We'll share a sanitized trace. Also question on quotas: can we reserve capacity by route or by token class, not just by customer? We have high-value routes that need guaranteed latency.

[30:05] Marco: Yes — route-level reservations are supported. You can attach routing policies per API key or per route. That maps to the priority queue so high-value routes can preempt lower class.

[32:15] Anita: Are there limitations on burst frequency? We expect up to 6-8 peaks per day short-lived.

[32:28] Marco: The main practical limit is how often you can scale because of cold-start impact on KV priming. Frequent back-to-back bursts will increase P99 until the cache warms. That's why we recommend maintaining a small warm buffer or using predictive ramping for known patterns.

[34:50] Gavin: Network constraints: during a burst we might hit egress policy limits on our side. Redwood peering — is there an option for private connectivity (direct connect) instead of public egress?

[34:59] Lena: Yes, we offer private connectivity options — VPC peering and dedicated interconnects via partners. We'll get network ops on a call if needed.

[36:10] Priya: Ok on acceptance criteria for pilot expansion: if we can keep P95 under 500ms and P99 under 1.2s while maintaining classification delta <1.5% for 24h burst at 3x baseline, we greenlight scale.

[36:30] Lena: Noted. We'll aim to produce the burst sim and the regression eval.

[38:20] Marco: Small note — we saw a weird transcribe in our last run where the KV cache was reported as k-v cash in logs. Just a reminder logs can be messy, so we'll attach raw traces and normalized readouts.

[40:00] Anita: Anything else on legal/compliance? We will need SOC2 docs and a DP processing addendum before production.

[40:10] Lena: We'll share SOC2 and DPA templates. Enterprise legal is ready to engage.

[42:05] Priya: Thanks. Final ask: include sample fallback latency timelines so we can present to product leadership.
[42:12] Lena: We'll include that in the write-up.

[43:00] Lena: Wrap up — recap of next steps and owners. Thanks all.

[43:20] Meeting end.
